title: Sandy Frank Dies: Legendary Distributor & ‘Name That Tune’ Producer Was 97
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter Druski Strikes Deal With Netflix Ahead Of ‘Collect & Praise’ Launch HBO’s ‘Big Little Lies’ Kicks Off Production On Season 3, Sort Of Paramount+ Names Damla Dogan As Unscripted Chief View All November 2, 2026 11:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sandy Frank Courtesy Sandy Frank , the veteran TV distributor and producer, has died at the age of 97. Frank is best known for producing and distributing game shows such as Name That Tune and The Dating Game as well as bringing Japanese monster movies to the United States. Starting out as a sales executive for Paramount Pictures in the late 1940s, Frank went on to work at NBC before becoming President of Worldwide Sales at Wrather Corporation, which produced and distributed Lassie and Lone Ranger. He subsequently launched Sandy Frank Program Sales, where he sold series including You Asked For It before also moving into production with Sandy Frank Entertainment (SFE). Related Stories News John Leeson Dies: Actor Who Voiced Iconic Role In 'Doctor Who' Was 83 News Marty Erlichman Dies: Barbra Streisand's Longtime Manager Was 97 Series he worked on included Name That Tune, Face The Music, The Parent Game and The Dating Game. Watch on Deadline Sandy Frank Entertainment also produced Battle of the Planets , a U.S. adaptation of the Japanese anime series Science Ninja Team Gatchaman, after discovering the series at Mip TV in Cannes. The series was an after-school hit throughout the 1970s. He was also well known for bringing other Japanese content to the U.S. including the Gamera films with a number of them including Fugitive Alien and Time of the Apes appearing on Mystery Science Theater 3000. Well known as a syndicator and distributor, Frank also funded a children’s orphanage in Cannes and would regularly arrange for Mip attendees, including buyers, to attend the orphanage during the market. “For over 50 years, SFE was synonymous with a take no prisoners style of television sales. Mr. Frank was a bigger-than-life TV executive. To say he was unrelenting and tenacious would be an understatement. The lengths Mr. Frank would go to make a sale were legendary [even] if it meant forcing a plane to land to get to a meeting or being relentlessly persistent until the TV station program buyer finally surrendered and made a deal,” said Frank’s longtime collaborator Bob Cohen. “Sandy Frank was the opposite character of the schlepper salesman Billy Loman in Death of a Salesman . Mr. Frank cut a glamorous style of a TV executive jet-setting around the globe, usually with the arm of a beautiful lady companion. Handsome, lean, fashionable, Mr. Frank left an indelible mark on modern TV production and distribution.” Frank’s proudest moment was acquiring the rights to Anwar Sadat’s autobiography with Sadat , the miniseries, produced in 1983 by Columbia Pictures with Frank becoming the first Jew to address the Egyptian Parliament. The executive also championed the cause of independent TV production by fighting the repeal of the Prime-Time Access Rule (PTAR). The PTAR limited the hours the networks could program, benefiting independent producers. “For those of us who loved him, he was caustic, manic, tough, generous, smart, fearless, sensitive, and a genius. He truly was one-of-a-kind, and his gravestone will read America’s Best TV Syndicator,” added Cohen. title: NFL and TMRW Sports’ Set ‘Premier Flag’ League Launch for Summer 2027
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All November 2, 2026 11:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Grace Amber Conway of Great Britain Photo by Pau Barrena/Getty Images The new flag football league from the NFL and TMRW Sports will officially launch next summer, and now it also has a name: Premier Flag. The league and the sports media company (which is also behind the TGL golf league) announced the new branding Monday. Premier Flag will get underway well ahead of the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, where the sport will be prominently featured. The NFL views flag football as a major growth engine, not only to get people interested in the full contact version of the game, but as a sport worth playing and watching in its own right. The inaugural season will be played in a purpose-built flag football stadium, the location of which is to be announced. Similarly, media rights for the first season are still being discussed, though the summer window gives it an opening, with only Major League Baseball as significant summertime competition (and a possible lockout may interrupt the next baseball season). “Flag football is exploding in popularity, and Premier Flag is establishing itself as the destination for the world’s top women and men competing at the highest level of the sport. The Premier Flag brand represents where flag football is headed – elite, global and accessible – while setting a professional standard for the sport’s growing ecosystem,” said Brendan Donohue, president of flag football for TMRW Sports. “When we launch next summer, fans will have the opportunity to see these amazing athletes perform at their best, supported by Premier Flag’s world-class training, strength and conditioning, nutrition and coaching programs.” “Premier Flag represents an exciting step forward in the continued evolution of flag football,” added Brian Flinn, NFL senior VP of global flag football. “Together with TMRW Sports, we’re building a global platform to showcase the world’s top flag football players and to engage fans in a premium experience, with the Premier Flag Showcase during Super Bowl LXI week providing an exciting first look at that vision. The launch of Premier Flag creates a new professional opportunity for the world’s best players and establishes the pinnacle of the sport’s growing global pathway.” The NFL and TMRW Sports officially announced the league earlier this year, with all 32 team owners invested alongside institutional investors and celebrity investors like Silver Lake, Ariel Investments/Project Level, Bessemer Venture Partners, Blue Pool Capital, and Dynasty Equity, as well as Tom Brady, Peyton Manning, Serena Williams, Billie Jean King, Joe Montana and Alex Morgan. In fact, Morgan’s TOGETHXR media and content company will provide social content strategy and production for the league, with Pivot Brand Group creating the brand name, positioning and visual identity of Premier Flag. title: Driven Unveils Original Programming Slate, Including Series Starring Tom Nelson, Emelia Hartford and Tanner Foust (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 2, 2026 11:01am PT Driven Unveils Original Programming Slate, Including Series Starring Tom Nelson, Emelia Hartford and Tanner Foust (EXCLUSIVE) By Jennifer Maas Plus Icon Jennifer Maas TV Business Writer @jmaasaronson Latest Driven Unveils Original Programming Slate, Including Series Starring Tom Nelson, Emelia Hartford and Tanner Foust (EXCLUSIVE) 7 minutes ago Sega’s ‘Sonic the Hedgehog’ to Launch Lingokids Games (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Future Games Show Sets Its First Live, In-Person Event During Gamescom 2027 (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Driven Automotive enthusiast-centric interactive streaming platform Driven has unveiled its initial original programming slate beginning with “Art of Speed” starring renowned engine builder Tom Nelson. First announced last December , Driven comes from car-enthusiast co-founders including longtime producer Michael George, “Top Gear USA” host Tanner Foust and “Gran Turismo” actor Emelia Hartford. Related Stories What's Driving Spanish TV? Spanish Drama Originals on Platforms, Renewals and Crossover Genres ‘Death in Paradise’ Gets Its First International Adaptation in Croatia, Promises 'Murder Mystery, Humor, Warmth and a Strong Sense of Place’ (EXCLUSIVE) Additional original series include programs starring automotive talent like Hartford (“Gran Turismo”), Foust (“Top Gear USA”), Ben Collins (“Top Gear”), Ant Anstead (“Wheeler Dealers”), Jenson Button (Formula 1 World Champion), Tom Nelson (renowned car builder), Antron Brown (award-winning drag racer) and more. Per Driven, this starting lineup will “anchor a library of content from established and emerging creators, and complement conversations in dedicated communities where enthusiasts can connect, discuss their interests, share projects, and exchange knowledge.” Driven unveiled its original series lineup ahead of its upfront presentation to advertisers, which is scheduled for Nov. 3 at SEMA in Las Vegas. According to the company, the platform’s initial beta program has brought in more than 15,000 users over the last few months and “helped shape the platform’s technology, features and community experience, with members continuing to influence its development.” The ad-supported, subscription-free platform is available on iOS, Android, web, Apple TV, Google TV, and Amazon Fire TV, with additional connected-TV platforms planned. “We built Driven to bring premium storytelling and authentic car culture together,” Driven CEO Michael George said. “Enthusiasts want to go deeper into the people, the craft and what’s really at stake. These four originals deliver that – without fabricated timelines, fake ticking clocks, or manufactured drama. The ambition, setbacks, and breakthroughs are real. Driven is giving those stories a home, and look forward to sharing them with our audience.” Additional series premiering exclusively on Driven in early 2027 will include “Pikes Peak” (starring Tanner Foust, Jenson Button and Ant Anstead), “Queen of the Mountain” (starring Emelia Hartford) and “Go or Go Home” (starring NHRA champion Antron Brown). Descriptions for each series, provided by Driven, can be found below. ART OF SPEED Six 1-hour episodes. Starring Tom Nelson. Created and Directed by Michael George. Produced by Emelia Hartford. Executive Produced by Michael George, Matt Swanson and Tom Lofthouse. The man behind the most powerful street cars on earth, and the over five years it took to build them. Tom Nelson left street racing to build a company around what he understood better than anyone: horsepower. Nelson Racing Engines became the place you go when 1,000 horsepower is the starting point, and the cars that roll out of his Chatsworth shop have gone on to Hollywood, to magazine covers and to the kind of owners who want something nobody else has. Art of Speed was shot over five years inside that shop. Each episode follows one build from a bare block to the first time its owner turns the key, including Maximus, the twin-turbo Charger built for Furious 7, and F-Bomb, David Freiburger’s 1,500-horsepower Camaro. The engines are the easy part. The hard part is everything around them: the deadlines, the customers, the physics, and a builder who has never once accepted the number on the dyno as the final answer. It ends in Iceland, with a machine on roads it was never meant for. PIKES PEAK Three 1-hour episodes. Starring Tanner Foust, Ant Anstead and Jenson Button. Directed by Tom Lofthouse and Dan Hack. Produced by Jake Cardew and Ed Sanders. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse. One hundred days to build a car. One mountain to prove it. A customer handed Radford Motors a million dollars and told them to build whatever they wanted. Ant Anstead decided to race it up America’s deadliest road before delivering it. One hundred days on the clock, a company that had never raced anything, and a car nobody had driven in anger. Ant and Jenson Button put Radford’s name on it. Joe Scarbo and Martin Jung built it. Tanner Foust, who has raced almost everything with wheels, agreed to take it up 12.42 miles of mountain with no barriers where it matters, in a car that was still being finished the week it shipped. No insurance if it crashes. No second attempt if it fails. Pikes Peak: A Race to the Clouds follows the whole thing, from a bare chassis in a California shop to practice mornings above the treeline, through the breakages, the all-nighters and the clashes, to a result nobody saw coming: Radford’s first race ever, and a win. QUEEN OF THE MOUNTAIN One 90-minute documentary. Starring DRIVEN co-founder Emelia Hartford. Featuring Jeff Zwart, Tanner Foust, Betim Berisha, and Robin Shute. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse. 12.42 miles. 156 corners. One run. The mountain decides. A year ago Pikes Peak sent DRIVEN co-founder Emelia Hartford home before the summit. So she built a car to go back: a brand new Corvette ZR1, 1,064 horsepower to the rear wheels, a cage she welded herself, and a crew she moved to Colorado for a month. Race week nearly broke the program. Her carbon wheels were banned mid-week, the car failed tech, and two days out she was tearing it apart to re-weld the cage while the coolant boiled over. Then the green flag. Ten minutes and eleven seconds later, she was the fastest woman ever up Pikes Peak, in the fastest rear-wheel-drive production car the mountain has seen, on her first run to the top in the race’s 104th year. Queen of the Mountain tells the story behind that time, featuring Jeff Zwart, the champion who coached her corner by corner, Tanner Foust, Betim Berisha, and Robin Shute, the veterans who know what fast really costs up there, and the question none of them can quite answer: why this road, at this price, every June. Emelia’s answer is already in. Just wait till next year. GO OR GO HOME Three 30-minute episodes. Starring Antron Brown. Directed by Ben Carter. Produced by Lisa Hughes Kennedy. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse. A season inside NHRA drag racing, where runs last under four seconds and every driver says goodbye to their family before strapping in. Top Fuel dragsters are the fastest accelerating machines on earth. Go or Go Home spends a season with the people who drive them and the people who pay for them: four-time champion Steve Torrence, who nearly died twice before he ever sat in a race car. Antron Brown, racing toward the win most drivers want, at Indy. And the young drivers and family-run teams trying to stay on the track against billionaire budgets. Shot across Bristol, Sonoma, Charlotte and the U.S. Nationals at Indianapolis, with full access to the pits and the homes behind them. The results are in there. What stays with you is the rest of it: fathers and sons, the money it takes, the fear nobody talks about, and the hour between rounds when a crew tears an engine down to nothing and rebuilds it. title: Marc Maron to Be Honored With Inaugural Richard Lewis Award at Comedy Gives Back Gala
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All November 2, 2026 10:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marc Maron attends the AFI Los Angeles premiere of 20th Century Studios' 'Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere' at Hollywood's TCL Chinese Theater on Oct. 22, 2025. (Photo by Jesse Grant/Getty Images for 20th Century Studios) Comedy Gives Back — a nonprofit founded by Jodi Lieberman, Amber J. Lawson and Zoe Friedman to provide a safety net for the comedy community — is finding another way to do so by launching its first ever gala in honor of the late Richard Lewis . The Richard Lewis Humor & Humanity Gala, dubbed “a night of comedy and neurosis,” is set to take place at Hollywood Improv in Los Angeles on Nov. 15. The organization will present an inaugural trophy that night as well, also called the Richard Lewis Humor & Humanity Award, in honor of his legacy and his years-long commitment to uplifting his peers. They’ve settled on the first recipient, Marc Maron , who will be feted at the event, which will be hosted by Jeff Garlin and feature Nick Kroll as a presenter. Related Stories News Jeff Garlin Considered Suicide After Tumultuous 'Goldbergs' Exit General News Publicist Emily Vespa Joins Birch Public Relations “Richard Lewis was one of a kind. He was fearless, painfully honest and could make you laugh about the things most people are afraid to talk about. To receive an award in his name is incredibly meaningful, especially knowing it supports comedians who need help,” said Maron in a statement. Lewis, who passed away at age 76 in February 2024, was an early supporter of Comedy Gives Back and he served as a member of the org’s board. The fundraiser will host comedy and entertainment insiders while raising money for the mission of providing financial assistance, mental health resources and addiction recovery support for comedians in need. “Richard wasn’t just a comedy legend. He was our friend and an early champion of Comedy Gives Back. We couldn’t imagine a more fitting first honoree than Marc Maron. This evening is about celebrating Richard’s incredible legacy while continuing his commitment to taking care of the comedy community,” said co-founders Lieberman, Lawson and Friedman in a joint statement. Maron, a veteran stand-up and actor, launched his podcast WTF With Marc Maron in 2009. After 16 years, he stepped away to focus on other endeavors like his acting career. He stars in Stick and recently appeared in the Bruce Springsteen biopic, Deliver Me From Nowhere. Comedy Gives Back’s Richard Lewis Humor & Humanity Gala is being sponsored by HBO and the Johnny Carson Foundation. More intel can be found here . THR

title: John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical ‘Romance & Cigarettes’ and the Knicks Championship
full_text: × Nov 2, 2026 10:46am PT John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical ‘Romance & Cigarettes’ and the Knicks Championship Awards Circuit Podcast: Turturro discusses his new role in the Sony Pictures Classics drama, plus the success of Apple TV's 'Severance' and more. By Clayton Davis Plus Icon Clayton Davis Chief Awards Editor byClaytonDavis Latest John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical ‘Romance & Cigarettes’ and the Knicks Championship 31 minutes ago ‘Obsession’ Breakout Inde Navarrette to Receive Rising Star Award at Palm Springs Film Awards (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Joel Coen’s ‘Jack of Spades,’ With Josh O’Connor and Patsy Ferran, Lands at Netflix for Fall 2027 2 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Primož Korošec John Turturro never actually picked a pocket on the subway, but he came close. “I had my hand, like, right, sort of almost in the bag,” he tells Variety . “But then I felt like, well, then I would have to give it back, and I could get arrested.” That is about as far as the star of “ The Only Living Pickpocket in New York ” was willing to take his homework, which he did under Apollo Robbins, the sleight-of-hand artist Turturro describes as part concert pianist, part psychologist. The rest of the practice happened on set, where he spent the shoot lifting things off the crew and occasionally getting caught. “The whole idea is that you don’t feel it,” he says. “It’s kind of a magic trick.” Related Stories Gersh Launches Victoria House, Expanding Into Scripted Films, True Crime and International Co-Productions (EXCLUSIVE) The Muppets Turn 50 This Year but They Nearly Didn't Get Made at All: 'It Was a Real Study in Perseverance' The film, written and directed by Rian Johnson regular Noah Segan, runs a tight 90 minutes and puts Turturro at the center as Harry, an aging thief caring for his disabled wife in a city that no longer has much use for him. Steve Buscemi, his co-star across “Miller’s Crossing,” “Barton Fink” and “The Big Lebowski,” and Giancarlo Esposito are along for the ride. Turturro, who has been a caretaker and a guardian himself, says the restraint is the point. “When someone goes for your jugular, sometimes you can recoil,” he says. “But when someone opens their heart up and offers it to you, it allows you space to enter.” It has been a strange and lovely year for him. The Knicks fan who fell for the 1969-70 and 1973 teams watched his franchise finally win another championship, and he is still shaking his head about it. He is 69 and looks a decade or two younger. Turturro is the only person in this awards conversation who has won best actor at Cannes, earned Emmy nominations for “The Night Of” and the Apple TV sci-fi drama “Severance” and never once heard his name read on Oscar nominations morning. “That’s the cherry on top of the cake,” he says of the accolades. “That’s not why you do it.” Turturro has a screenplay of Philip Roth’s “Sabbath’s Theater” waiting for people brave enough to make it. And he is still chasing the film he has wanted to make for years, an adaptation of Susan Sheehan’s Pulitzer Prize-winning “Is There No Place on Earth for Me?,” a book about mental illness and the families it splinters that he knows, he says, “really well personally.” “As you get older, time is precious,” he says. “I believe in the audience, and I believe in the young audience, too.” On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast , Turturro discusses his new role in the Sony Pictures Classics drama, why he’s still proud of “Romance & Cigarettes,” the 2005 musical he had to buy back and release himself after a studio regime change, and more. Listen below! The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity. John Turturro in “The Only Living PIckpocket in New York” Courtesy of MRC II Distribution Company Have you ever actually pickpocketed anyone? I did a lot when I was practicing with Apollo Robbins. He’s a magician and a pickpocket, and he basically gave me a course. He’s kind of a psychologist. He understands how someone approaches another person, from the social sphere to the personal to the intimate. What he can do with his hands is like a concert pianist. He gave me exercises and things to do. I didn’t really pickpocket anyone on the subway, but I came close. I had my hand almost in someone’s bag. But then I thought, well, I’d have to give it back, and I could get arrested. I practiced a lot on set, constantly trying to do it with the crew. Sometimes you’d get caught. The whole idea is that you don’t feel it. It’s kind of a magic trick. Noah Segan was an actor before becoming a director. What’s different about working with someone who understands what it’s like to be in front of the camera? It helps, but I’ve worked with a lot of actor-directors, and they’re all different. He’s not cynical. He’s an open-hearted fellow. He wrote the script, and what I brought to it was my offering. He was very open to things. He gave me a playlist of songs he listened to, and I used a lot of them on the set. He was really delicate. The cinematographer, Sam Levy, who was Harris Savides’ assistant, brought in these old lenses from the ’70s. We did tests with them, and that’s why the movie has that kind of ’70s vibe. We wanted to find the most intimate way to shoot it without an extreme amount of cutting. You and Steve Buscemi have worked together for more than 30 years. How much of that chemistry comes from friendship versus acting? You have a history. I have a history with Giancarlo, too, but not as long as with Steve. There’s a comfort zone and a shorthand. You can build off that and take advantage of it. They’re both wonderful actors, and that makes the fabric of the film really rich. Harry is caring for his disabled wife in a city that doesn’t really need him anymore. The film is deeply emotional but never sentimental. How did you find that balance? There was something innately resonant in the film when I read it. You’re of a certain age, so you’ve experienced success and failure. You know what it is to be surrounded by loss. My phone is surrounded by a lot of ghosts. And being a husband, a son and a father, there are always regrets and mistakes you make, even when you try your best. I know from being a caretaker myself, a guardian, sometimes in extreme situations, that it’s not a celebrated thing. You can be upset, but you’re giving to someone else. You’re putting your attention on the other person, and you’re doing it for them. It’s not about you. The film creeps up on you emotionally. I’ve seen it a few times and seen the effect it has on people. Rian Johnson told me it gets him every time. There’s a restraint that allows you to feel something. When someone goes for your jugular, sometimes you can recoil. But when someone opens their heart up and offers it to you, it allows you space to enter. I’m from the Bronx. I grew up watching John Starks and Patrick Ewing walk off without a ring. And you’re on an Oscar run the year the Knicks finally win the championship. Do you feel like you can do anything now? I loved the team when I was a kid, in ’69 and ’70, and they went again in ’73. That was my team, and I became a loyal Knicks fan. The afterglow hasn’t left. I love the way they did it. There’s a kind of chemistry. They’re almost overachievers, most of them on the team, and that made everything even sweeter. The way they kept coming back, led by our fearless captain, Jalen Brunson. This little guy with incredible footwork and smarts, and how he can read a game. It felt like one of the few real team victories. This was a team, a real team victory, and that’s beautiful in life because people don’t celebrate the collective. It really takes the collective to accomplish things. It’s the same way when you do a movie. Everything has to work together, because one thing can really mess it up. It’s been a lovely year. What can I say? You’ve won best actor at Cannes for “Barton Fink,” earned Emmy nominations for “The Night Of” and “Severance” and never received an Oscar nomination. Does that register with you? This has been a very rich time for me, a wonderful career. I didn’t know I was going to work with all different kinds of people who would give me different opportunities. I’ve worked with so many great directors, so I’m very appreciative of the career I have. Accolades, I’ve gotten some things. That’s the cherry on top of the cake. That’s not why you do it. My objective is to tell a story and reach you, whether it’s through comedy, drama or both. To move you, to make you identify with the plight of the character. I’m competitive mostly with myself. Would it be nice to be acknowledged? Yes. If it gets more people to see the movie, that’s even better. I’m a huge fan of “Romance & Cigarettes.” Do you ever think about getting back behind the camera? With “Romance & Cigarettes,” we had a great distributor lined up. It was United Artists, but United Artists and MGM got bought by Sony. Bingham Ray was the person who greenlit it. When the new people came in, Joel and Ethan Coen were my executive producers, and they had final cut. They said, “When you see the movie, it’s a new comedy. Please see it with an audience.” But they had a couple of old geezers who saw it, and they just didn’t understand the movie. So I got stuck in limbo with a film we’d tested and were preparing for an 800-theater release. I fought to get it back and put together some money, including some of my own, to distribute it. We got a tremendous response from critics, and in some countries it played for a really long time. That’s something I’m quite proud of. There are exceptional things in that movie. “Severance” introduced you to a generation that might not know your earlier work. What do you think has made the series resonate? We never know. I think the success was the execution by Ben Stiller, and Dan Erickson posed the question about having your brain split. Something about that resonated post-COVID, even though we shot it during COVID. You don’t know what’s going to resonate with people. It’s a wonderful group of people, and I’ve gotten to work with Christopher Walken, which was sort of my idea. Shows like this pose a question, and I’m interested in how you answer it. How do you survive this inside and outside? You have a screenplay of Philip Roth’s “Sabbath’s Theater” and have been trying to adapt Susan Sheehan’s Pulitzer Prize-winning book “Is There No Place on Earth for Me?” What keeps those projects alive for you? I have the rights and the screenplay for “Sabbath’s Theater,” which is pretty wild, racy, about sex and death. I just have to find people who will be brave enough to do it. We tested it with an audience as a play, and it played really well. I’ve also wanted to do “Is There No Place on Earth for Me?” for many years. It’s about mental illness, and I have a lot of experience with that, unfortunately. But it’s not what you would think, because it has the whole person in it. It’s not just the disease. It’s the family and the labyrinth of the mental health system, which I know really well personally. I was going to do it as a miniseries, but it’s a difficult subject because people always want a story where someone gets better. The idea is that someone can find a level of peace, and that the family can stay together. A lot of families are splintered by it and very isolated. These are real people who suffer. They have tremendous dimension and capacity for manipulation, lust, ambition and rage. They’re full human beings. That’s something I would love to get a crack at. You’re 69, and you look 40. Has the way you decide which projects are worth your time changed? I always was sort of picky, maybe stupidly at times. I tried to save my money when I first started, because I’d done interesting plays, and I would turn things down. In those days, you could make a nice living in a middle-sized film, and I never did big films until 2000 or so. As you get older, time is precious, and the things I really want to do, I don’t want to give that up. I have confidence in the audience. Sometimes the gatekeepers can help you, or they’re an obstacle, but I think audiences are hungry to see different kinds of things. I really do. I believe in the audience, and I believe in the young audience, too. title: Sacha Baron Cohen Talks Tarantino, AI & Why Undercover Comedy ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Will Be His Last — Comedy Means Business Podcast
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt Stephen McKinley Henderson To Topline Crime Drama ‘Anglers’ From Debut Filmmaker Zoe Simone Sacha Baron Cohen Talks Tarantino, AI & Why Undercover Comedy ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Will Be His Last — Comedy Means Business Podcast Isabela Merced & Patrick Schwarzenegger To Play Lorena And John Bobbitt In Hulu’s ‘Good American Family’ Anthology View All November 2, 2026 10:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source There’s an apocryphal quote attributed to the late, great George Carlin: “It’s the duty of the comedian to find out where the line is drawn and cross it deliberately.” If that’s true, few have crossed it more frequently—or more fearlessly—than Sacha Baron Cohen . Very few, also, have had the global impact in feature comedy that he has had. Over the last three decades, Cohen has permeated global pop culture with a range of original characters. In particular, Ali G , his faux-streetwise cultural appropriator from Staines-upon-Thames, and Borat, his blundering Kazakh journalist, have helped drive cultural conversation, even as the work has provoked backlash in equal measure to laughter. Related Stories News Jack Lowden On James Bond & Gary Oldman's 007 Endorsement: "It's All Very Flattering" News 'The Man With The Bag' Trailer: Arnold Schwarzenegger & Alan Ritchson Star In Amazon MGM's Christmas Heist Caper Inclined until recently to let his characters speak for themselves, Cohen has generally taken the public’s response in stride, committed to the goal of helping to “make a slightly more tolerant society” through satire. A master of disguise, whose disruptive influence on comedy dates back to ’90s London, his M.O. has been to send meticulously crafted, memorably buffoonish characters careening through the real world. The goal? To expose the assumptions, prejudices and absurdities of those interacting with them in the real world — whether on the right or left, in a position of tremendous power or someone off the street. Watch on Deadline The work that goes into these films, and the stakes behind them are immense; repeatedly, across projects, Cohen has put his life on the line for the sake of a joke. Naturally, then, he’s spoken on more than one occasion about retiring from his work in undercover comedy. He makes the claim, once again, while discussing his latest feature, Ali G: Who Iz I? — his first film centered on the character in more than 20 years, and his first as director. If this is indeed Cohen’s last outing with his experimental form of filmmaking, he’s gone out with a bang. He calls Who Iz I? his “most extreme and ambitious” movie to date — his version of The Avengers , as a film in which he inhabit multiple of his characters. Not just his breakout character, Ali G, but also two of his creations for Showtime series Who Is America? : the obnoxious ultra-liberal Dr. Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, who becomes the Dr. Evil to Ali G’s Austin Powers, as well as the Israeli anti-terrorism expert Erran Morad. (Notably, Cohen even consulted with Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, the screenwriters behind Avengers: Endgame and myriad other MCU projects, in constructing his narrative.) Released last month, Who Iz I? finds Ali G resurfacing decades after the cancellation of Da Ali G Show when he learns that his girlfriend Julie (Morgana Robinson) is pregnant and he must find a way to support his family. When Nira Cain-N’Degeocello learns of the return of the “white culture appropriator,” he makes it his mission to get him canceled. The film culminates in a sequence shot continuously over eight hours and 12 locations, involving nearly 200 crew members and hundreds of carefully choreographed beats. To achieve it, Cohen brought in specialists in prosthetics, animatronics and explosives, alongside magicians and world-famous psychologists. “The end scene is, according to [VFX supervisor] Rob Legato, the most difficult scene ever shot,” Cohen tells me on today’s episode of Comedy Means Business , “and he worked on Titanic .” On this week’s podcast, Cohen shares the backstory behind his decision to bring Ali G back, before getting into the extreme prep that’s made his films possible. We also discuss his career beginnings, and how his early academic work and lifelong interest in identity have fueled his films from Ali G Indahouse on — works whose intentions can be easily misinterpreted, which have more on their mind than some give them credit for. Explaining how each of his character comedies has been approached with a different genre in mind — Who Iz I? is a fugitive thriller — Cohen talks pressing through fear on set, navigating the online discourse around his work, and the unsettling recent “move towards the acceptance of political violence” that inspired his latest film. Also: his studies under iconic French clowning guru Philippe Gaulier, who passed away this year; his concerns surrounding AI; mastering sword fighting for his new play The Popinjay Cavalier , marking a long-in-the-works collaboration with Quentin Tarantino; and more. title: John Goodman Says ‘Digger’ Was ‘Killed’ by Critics ‘Before We Even Opened’ and ‘It Hurt’
full_text: × Nov 2, 2026 10:23am PT John Goodman Says ‘Digger’ Was ‘Killed’ by Critics ‘Before We Even Opened’ and ‘It Hurt’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest John Goodman Says ‘Digger’ Was ‘Killed’ by Critics ‘Before We Even Opened’ and ‘It Hurt’ 41 minutes ago Jennifer Lawrence Says ‘Absolutely F—ing Not’ to Transforming Into X-Men’s Mystique Again 3 days ago Jessica Lange Hints at Acting Retirement: ‘I Feel Like I’m Coming to an End… It Doesn’t Seem Easy to Get Things Made Anymore’ 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Seoju Park /© Warner Bros. /Courtesy Everett Collection John Goodman is finally speaking out about “ Digger ” flopping with critics and at the box office. During an appearance on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, the actor said all of the negative pre-release buzz for the movie effectively killed its chances of making money at the box office. “Digger” cost north of $160 million to make and only earned $15 million in its domestic box office debut. The movie has yet to cross $50 million worldwide after one month in theaters. Related Stories The Muppets Turn 50 This Year but They Nearly Didn't Get Made at All: 'It Was a Real Study in Perseverance' What's Driving Spanish TV? Spanish Drama Originals on Platforms, Renewals and Crossover Genres “People are talking. It hurt. It kinda killed us before we even opened. [The headlines like]: ‘This will only make $5.’ It was good reason for people to avoid it,” Goodman said about the response. “I am proud of it. I had a ball doing it. It was a good six months out of my life. It is a huge swing. It’s going to be around for a long time.” When asked if he still cares about what critics and audiences think of his work after so many years as a professional actor, Goodman responded: “Unfortunately I have to say that I am. I have to be very honest. I used to be less so. Maybe I am getting old and pathetic and it’s like, ‘Don’t hit me again!’ I put so much into this film and here you go. I am over it now. I am proud I did it.” However, Goodman noted that “everything I have done for the Coen Brothers flopped initially… so who cares, man? I still have people coming up to me in the streets asking me about ‘Barton Fink’ and ‘Big Lebowski.'” Goodman starred opposite Tom Cruise in “Digger,” directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu. Cruise plays an oil tycoon who is faced with the end of the world after one of his rigs in Antartica malfunctions and sends ice caps hurtling towards Europe. Goodman stars as the U.S. president. The movie strongly divided critics (53% on Rotten Tomatoes) and needed an estimated $350 million just to break even in theaters. It will now go down as one of the most costly studio flops in Hollywood history by losing Warner Bros. around $250 million in theaters. Amid the movie’s disastrous box office run, various Hollywood celebrities rallied around Cruise and the movie. Neil Young posted on his website that “Digger” is “the best film I have ever seen.” Mandy Patinkin agreed, hailing Cruise’s latest as an “instant classic” and “one of the greatest pieces of film I have ever seen in my entire life.” Anne Hathaway, Jane Fonda, Ben Affleck and more also sung the movie’s praises, with Affleck condemning the public bashing of the movie. “Everybody wants to celebrate this bomb as if it’s the most exciting thing to happen. And you think like, it’s a pretty ambitious, interesting movie made by interesting people who have talent,” Affleck said in his own “Happy Sad Confused” interview last month. “Everybody wants to count the money, what it lost or whatever. To me, I just think, if you punish movies that take risks, guess what you’re going to get? A bunch of shitty homogenized movies. You cannot do something interesting without taking a big swing. And that means you’re going to sometimes look bad.” Watch Goodman’s full interview on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast below. title: Like, Subscribe, Graduate: Emerson College Launching Content Creation Major (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All November 2, 2026 9:52am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Henry Winkler speaks at Emerson College's 2026 commencement ceremony in Boston. Photo by Lisa Aileen Dragani/Getty Images Communications students matriculating into Emerson College next year will have an entirely new major to choose from: A bachelor of arts in content creation. The Hollywood Reporter has learned that the Boston-based college will launch the new degree program in the fall of 2027. The new degree underscores the rapidly changing dynamics of media, with creator-led platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram continuing to grow at a rapid clip even as traditional film and TV production and distribution seems to be flat or declining. The new major will pull from the school’s existing infrastructure and expertise in areas like storytelling, production and communications while incorporating creator-focused areas of study like marketing, audience development, branding and business strategy, given the owner-operator nature of the creator world. Students will develop original content while studying the business and ethics of digital platforms, while also learning how to reach and engage audiences. “Emerson has long prepared students for success in emerging creative industries with a focus on hands-on, real world application in our academic disciplines and now this new major builds on our tradition by combining creativity, technology and entrepreneurial skills for the next generation,” said Emerson president Jay Bernhardt. Emerson, which is among THR’s 25 best film schools of 2026, has an envious alumni list that includes former Warner Bros. film co-chief Pamela Abdy, filmmakers Daniel Kwan and Paul Thomas Anderson, writer Norman Lear and actors like Henry Winkler and Jennifer Coolidge. The bachelor of arts in content creation will be housed in Emerson College’s School of Communication, within the department of strategic marketing and business. “Our new content creation major prepares students to be a part of the evolving creator economy , teaching them not only how to produce compelling digital content but also how to build a successful entrepreneurial career,” said Brenna McCormick, chair of the department of strategic marketing and business. “From digital and financial literacy to business and marketing, this major has the essential ingredients to help students turn their creative visions into something bigger.” THR

title: Indigenous Documentary ‘Ceremony’ Lands at Netflix
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 2, 2026 9:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Ceremony' smayaykila-films Netflix has nabbed the Indigenous feature documentary Ceremony after a SXSW world premiere. Director Bianchi Hanuse’s film will land on the streamer in 2027 after winning awards at SXSW, Hot Docs and the Sydney Film Festival. Ceremony centers on British Columbia’s Nuxalk Nation as it looks to restore the local population of ooligan fish, whose arrival every spring sustains the First Nations community and its ritual celebrations. The restoration efforts, including broadcasts from the Nuxalk Radio station, also underline the resilience of the Indigenous community in the face of challenges from climate change and colonialization. “Nuxalkmc [Nuxalk people] asked for this story to be told and that responsibility took 12 years because our truth isn’t an easy one to tell. It’s a story most Canadians have never heard. We made it for us and with Netflix, we’re sharing it beyond our valley,” director Hanuse said in a statement. Related Stories Movies Netflix Acquires Joel Coen's 'Jack of Spades,' Planning Big Push for Next Oscar Season TV Druski Signs Deal With Netflix, Sets Church Comedy 'Collect & Praise' In Canada , Netflix has acquired earlier Indigenous-themed or directed content, including the late Jeff Barnaby’s Rhymes for Ghouls , Stephen S. Campanelli’s Indian Horse and Miranda de Pencier’s The Grizzlies . In 2024, Netflix acquired the documentary Yintah, which follows Indigenous activists with the Wet’suwet’en First Nation looking to protect their lands and was directed by Michael Toledano, Jennifer Wickham and Brenda Mitchell. Netflix also streams the Arctic-set Indigenous comedy North of North , a co-production with the CBC. That ongoing support for Indigenous movies and creators also comes amid calls by local indie producers and other cultural nationalists for Netflix and other U.S. tech giants and foreign players to be subject to the same content expenditure obligations as traditional broadcasters. Ceremony is written by Hanuse and Jessica Mayhew and is produced by Smayaykila Films. THR

title: Golden Globes: ‘Club Kid’ Submitted as Drama (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All November 2, 2026 9:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jordan Firstman and Reggie Absolom in 'Club Kid' Courtesy of A24 Club Kid , Jordan Firstman ’s acclaimed film about a club promoter who stays too long at the party, has been submitted by distributor A24 for Golden Globes consideration as a drama, rather than a musical/comedy, The Hollywood Reporter has exclusively learned. This classification means that the film — which Firstman wrote, directed (as his feature directorial debut) and stars in — will compete in the genre-specific Globes categories (picture, actor and actress) against the likes of The Odyssey , La Bola Negra , Dune: Part Three , Elsinore , All of a Sudden , Fjord and Possible Love , rather than Wild Horse Nine , The Invite , The Debut , Artificial , Obsession , Project Hail Mary and Tender Loving Care . Related Stories General News 2026 Daytime Emmy Awards: 'General Hospital' Wins Best Daytime Drama TV The Hollywood Reporter Wins 2026 Daytime Emmy Award A24’s decision, which was made in close consultation with Firstman, may come as a surprise to some given Firstman’s background in comedy and the fact that some have described Club Kid as an elevated variation of Big Daddy , the 1999 Adam Sandler comedy about a man who unexpectedly becomes the guardian of a young child. But Club Kid becomes considerably more dramatic as it progresses, and Firstman — who shines in a decidedly dramatic courtroom scene late in the film — has cited heavier films like 1978’s An Unmarried Woman and 1979’s Kramer vs. Kramer as key inspirations. Club Kid had its world premiere at the Cannes Film Festival in the Un Certain Regard section, after which it received a seven-minute standing ovation and sparked an overnight bidding war among distributors. The film ultimately sold to A24 for $17 million, making it the biggest sale of the fest. It has since played to raves at the Telluride, Toronto, New York and other film fests. And it will begin a platform theatrical release on Friday. THR recently broke the news of two other high-profile Globes categorizations: Obsession as a musical/comedy and Artificial as a musical/comedy . THR

title: ‘Obsession’ Breakout Inde Navarrette to Receive Rising Star Award at Palm Springs Film Awards (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 2, 2026 9:20am PT ‘Obsession’ Breakout Inde Navarrette to Receive Rising Star Award at Palm Springs Film Awards (EXCLUSIVE) By Clayton Davis Plus Icon Clayton Davis Chief Awards Editor byClaytonDavis Latest John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical ‘Romance & Cigarettes’ and the Knicks Championship 31 minutes ago ‘Obsession’ Breakout Inde Navarrette to Receive Rising Star Award at Palm Springs Film Awards (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Joel Coen’s ‘Jack of Spades,’ With Josh O’Connor and Patsy Ferran, Lands at Netflix for Fall 2027 2 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Chad Salvador/Variety Inde Navarrette , the breakout star of Focus Features’ horror blockbuster “ Obsession ,” will receive the Rising Star Award at the Palm Springs International Film Awards, Variety has learned exclusively. Navarrette joins the growing list of honorees that already includes Seth Rogen, Olivia Wilde, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton, who share the Vanguard Award for “The Invite.” The film premiered to rave reviews, holds a 94% score on Rotten Tomatoes and has grossed more than $500 million worldwide, the largest gor a Focus Features release. It recently picked up a Gotham Award nomination, and critics have consistently singled out Navarrette’s gripping and emotionally charged turn, which has put her firmly in the Oscar race for best actress. Related Stories Mediawan's Pierre-Antoine Capton on Buying Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine and Doubling Down on Hollywood Amid Consolidation (EXCLUSIVE) Apple TV's Hit German Series 'Where’s Wanda?' Returns for Season 2, Again Asking: 'How Far Would You Go to Save Your Child?' Horror has historically struggled to break through with Academy voters, but has seemingly made a positive, more inclusive turn in recent years with “The Substance,” “Sinners” and “Weapons.” A Palm Springs honor is a critical stop on the Oscar campaign trail. The Rising Star Award itself has a strong track record as an Oscar bellwether. Past recipients include Ariana Grande for “Wicked,” Timothée Chalamet for “Call Me by Your Name,” Alicia Vikander for “The Danish Girl,” Jennifer Lawrence for “Winter’s Bone,” Anna Kendrick for “Up in the Air” and Scarlett Johansson for “Lost in Translation.” Grande, Chalamet, Vikander, Lawrence and Kendrick all went on to Academy Award nominations for those performances, with Vikander taking home the supporting actress statuette. “Inde Navarrette delivers a performance in ‘Obsession’ that is impossible to look away from,” Nachhattar Singh Chandi, festival chairman says in a statement. “She brings a rare combination of emotional awareness and cinematic presence to the screen. The Rising Star Award exists to celebrate exactly this kind of breakthrough talent, and we could not be more excited to welcome Inde to Palm Springs.” Written, edited and directed by Curry Barker, the indie thriller follows Bear, a hopeless romantic who breaks the mysterious One Wish Willow to win over his crush, only to find that getting exactly what he wants comes at a sinister price. Navarrette plays Nikki Freeman opposite Michael Johnston, Megan Lawless, Cooper Tomlinson and Andy Richter. Navarrette first broke out in the fourth and final season of Netflix’s teen drama “13 Reasons Why” before landing a series regular role on The CW’s superhero drama “Superman & Lois.” She made her Sundance debut in 2020 opposite Sienna Miller and Diego Luna in “Wander Darkly.” Navarrette is set to take on the iconic role of Rogue in Marvel’s upcoming “X-Men” film and will star in and executive produce “The Waffle House Index,” a sci-fi thriller from Apple Original Films and Plan B Entertainment. title: Netflix Acquires Joel Coen’s ‘Jack of Spades,’ Planning Big Push for Next Oscar Season
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All November 2, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joel Coen Stephane Cardinale - Corbis/Corbis via Getty Images Netflix has a full plate for this Oscar season — its contenders include La Bola Negra , 14th , Possible Love , Ray Gunn , Ink , Gentle Monster , The Mosquito Bowl , Avedon and In Waves — but that hasn’t stopped the streamer from making plans for next Oscar season, as well. The streamer has acquired the worldwide distribution rights to Joel Coen ’s next directorial outing, Jack of Spades , which is based on Frances Frederica Montrésor’s 1901 novel The Alien: A Story of Middle Age and is being described as “a sinister gothic mystery filled with intrigue and betrayal set in the atmospheric Scottish Highlands.” The film, which wrapped production earlier this year, will be released in theaters in fall 2027 ahead of its release on the platform. And the company sees it as a major awards prospect. Related Stories TV Druski Signs Deal With Netflix, Sets Church Comedy 'Collect & Praise' Business Netflix Layoffs Hit U.K., With VP, Production Anna Mallett Among 2-3 Percent of Staff Affected The film stars the 36-year-old Olivier Award winner Patsy Ferran , as well as Golden Globe winner Josh O’Connor, Golden Globe winner Damian Lewis and Oscar nominee Lesley Manville . Joel Coen wrote it with his brother Ethan (both won multiple Oscars for 2007’s No Country for Old Men ), as well as Eleanor Catton and Conor McPherson; and produced it with his wife, Frances McDormand (who won an Oscar for producing 2020’s Nomadland , and also was a producer on her husband’s 2021 film The Tragedy of Macbeth ), as well as Indian Paintbrush’s Steven Rales, Blueprint Pictures’ Graham Broadbent and Peter Czernin, and Robert Graf. The film’s crew includes numerous frequent collaborators of Joel Coen, among them cinematographer Bruno Delbonnel (2013’s Inside Llewyn Davis , The Tragedy of Macbeth and 2018’s The Ballad of Buster Scruggs ) and composer Carter Burwell (1984’s Blood Simple , 1987’s Raising Arizona , 1990’s Miller’s Crossing , 1991’s Barton Fink , 1994’s The Hudsucker Proxy , 1996’s Fargo , 1998’s The Big Lebowski , 2000’s O Brother, Where Art Thou? , 2001’s The Man Who Wasn’t There , 2003’s Intolerable Cruelty , 2004’s The Ladykillers , No Country for Old Men , 2008’s Burn After Reading , 2009’s A Serious Man , 2010’s True Grit , 2016’s Hail, Caesar! , The Ballad of Buster Scruggs and The Tragedy of Macbeth ). Jack of Spades marks a reunion between Netflix and Joel Coen following The Ballad of Buster Scruggs , which landed three Oscar noms, including best adapted screenplay for the Coen brothers; and between Netflix and Josh O’Connor following The Crown (2019-2020) and 2025’s Wake Up Dead Man . The Coen brothers are represented by UTA and attorney Pat Murphy. UTA represented the sale. THR

title: Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell Set for Kennedy Center Honors
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 2, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell JC Olivera/Getty Images; Phillip Faraone/Getty Images; Rodin Eckenroth/Getty Images; Ernesto Ruscio/Getty Images; Larry McCormack/Variety/Getty Images The latest honorees for the revamped Kennedy Center Honors have been unveiled. This year’s honorees are singers Paul Anka and Barbara Mandrell, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and writer David Mamet, it was announced on Monday. The latest Kennedy Center Honors will take place at Capital One Arena in Washington, D.C. The Kennedy Center itself has been at the center of a legal battle as U.S. President Donald Trump slammed a court decision to block his name, twice, from being added to the building’s exterior. The board at the arts institution also chose to shut down the Kennedy Center, with Trump in social media posts suggesting the closure would allow future renovations. Related Stories Music Bryan Adams Releases New Trump Protest Song "Lake Ontario" Music Neil Young Sues Trump for Using "Rockin' in the Free World" at Rally: "The Opposite of Everything Donald J. Trump Stands For" Launched in 1978, the annual Kennedy Center Honors event recognizes individuals who have made lifetime contributions to American culture through the performing arts. “We are recognizing amazing artists whose lifelong work has shaped American culture and inspired generations of audiences. We are proud to honor this year’s class and to continue a tradition that has defined the Center for nearly 50 years,” Trump said in a statement. There’s no word on whether Trump will again host the 2026 Kennedy Center Honors event. The ratings for the 2025 Kennedy Center Honors, hosted by Trump at the Kennedy Center, dropped to a new all-time low. Last year’s honors gala aired on CBS and Paramount+ amid news of Trump’s plans to rename the Kennedy Center to The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts. The push to rename the arts institution has drawn blowback, including by members of the Kennedy family and resulted in numerous artists dropping out of planned performance at the Kennedy Center. THR

title: Utopai Studios Names Former Disney AI Exec Hans Ku Chief Product Officer
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Elon Musk’s SpaceX Reportedly Talking With EchoStar About A Boost Mobile Deal Hello Sunshine Lays Off Half Of Staff In Wake Of Acquisition By Reese Witherspoon And Mediawan Reddit Shares Plunge 30% After Company Says Its Q3 Search Traffic Was “Down Meaningfully” View All November 2, 2026 9:08am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hans Ku Courtesy EXCLUSIVE: Hans Ku , a former Disney , DreamWorks and Yahoo exec, has been named Chief Product Officer at Utopai Studios . In his new post, Ku will lead product, engineering, research and business development. He will aim to increase the scale of the technology behind the emerging firm’s film and TV slate along with expanding the company’s cinematic storytelling engine. Ku most recently had been VP of AI & Engineering in Disney’s Office of Technology Enablement. He played a key role in Disney’s connection with OpenAI around the well-funded start-up’s generative video offering, Sora. At the end of 2025, Disney swung a deal with OpenAI to license characters for use on Sora in exchange for a $1 billion equity investment. The arrangement was later undone after Sora was shuttered. Related Stories Legal WME Urges "Ethical & Responsible" AI In NYT Copyright Battle With Sam Altman News Reddit Shares Plunge 30% After Company Says Its Q3 Search Traffic Was "Down Meaningfully" Prior to his AI stint at Disney, Ku also worked at Walt Disney Deature Animation, where he created a system to help traditional animators online. As an exec at DreamWorks Animation, he also created the DreamColor display in collaboration with HP, which netted him a Scientific and Engineering Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. Watch on Deadline In addition to those entertainment-oriented roles, Ku has also been an entrepreneur and a product exec at Tubi, Yahoo and TikTok predecessor Flipagram. Utopai Studios, founded in 2022, recently raised $60 million in funding at a $1 billion valuation. It is among the firms benefiting from the industry’s gradually increasing willingness to embrace AI (albeit within certain parameters) after the technology had initially set off alarms about job losses. “Hans knows what it takes to move emerging technology from experimentation into an organization operating at global scale,” said Cecilia Shen, CEO and co-founder of Utopai Studios, in a statement. “From developing tools for animators early in his career to helping lead Disney’s collaboration with OpenAI on Sora, Hans has consistently worked at the intersection of creative ambition and emerging technology. He brings that experience to a studio where filmmakers and technology teams develop tools together on active productions. That combination is critical to where Utopai Studios is going next. We are building a global studio for a new era of entertainment, and Hans will be central to scaling the technology and infrastructure that make that possible.” Utopai “has the opportunity to build something fundamentally different because the studio and the technology are growing together,” Ku said. “We can take what we learn from real productions, turn those lessons directly into better products and workflows, and then bring those capabilities to filmmakers and studios around the world. title: Lexington Film Office Launches Workforce Development Initiative With Location Managers Guild

FilmLEX , the city’s official film and entertainment office, has partnered with the Location Mangers Guild International for a workforce development initiative, “From Page to Place: The Art of Location Management.” The two-day workshop is aimed at a wide range of skill levels, including college and high school students, emerging talent and local crew members. The event will take place November 6 and 7, and attendees will have access to LMGI professionals including Andrea Keener ( Killers of the Flower Moon , Captain America: Brave New World) , Todd Christensen ( The Hunger Games, Sicario ), Mike Fantasia ( Top Gun: Maverick, Killers of the Flower Moon ), and Dennis Muscari ( Oppenheimer, Breaking Bad ). Over the course of the two days, participants will engage in industry discussions, hands-on training, mentorship and networking. Related Stories News IATSE Taps Jillian Arnold As Union's First Labor & Technology Intelligence Officer News Hollywood Unions Warn U.S. Film & TV Production Is On The Brink In Latest Economic Report “It’s a tremendous privilege to partner with the Location Managers Guild International and have some of the industry’s most respected professionals helping us cultivate the next generation of talent right here in Central Kentucky,” Lisa Brin, Head of FilmLEX, said in a statement. “This is an exciting first step in strengthening the dynamic local production workforce and laying the foundation for long-term industry growth in Central Kentucky – one that we are deeply invested in.” Watch on Deadline Per FilmLEX, students from eight regional colleges and universities will participate, including University of Kentucky, Asbury University, Bluegrass Community & Technical College, Centre College, Eastern Kentucky University, Kentucky State University, Midway University, Transylvania University, as well as area high schools. Adds Danny Finn, President of the Locations Manager Guild International: “The future of our industry depends on investing in the next generation. Location professionals connect storytelling with the communities that make it possible and partnerships like this one with FilmLEX help introduce new talent to our craft while building the local workforce needed to sustain production for years to come.” The latest workshop is part of a broader initiative to strengthen the area’s local production workforce and build the necessary infrastructure to support a robust film and television industry in Central Kentucky. A major part of that effort is to build a deeper pool of skilled production professionals across a range of disciplines, including location management, producing, assistant directing, production design, editorial and on-camera talent. Lexington ’s convention and visitor’s bureau launched FilmLEX two years ago to promote Kentucky ’s incentive program, which launched in 2022, and help producers on the ground. The official announcement of FilmLEX called Lexington “a modern, mid-size city rich in history and resources for the filmmaking community. The area boasts abundantly diverse landscapes and real-life backdrops that serve as a façade for any genre — from bustling, urban cityscapes to quaint small towns frozen in time; and from rolling bluegrass hills and lush forests to castles, battlefields and abandoned rickhouses [used to store bourbon]. Lexington’s four seasons create mood and personality all year round with best-in-class hospitality and a warm and welcoming spirit.” Local celebrities Steve Zahn and Rick Gomez, who founded Macaroni Art Productions in Midway just outside of Lexington, have long been supporters of bolstering the state’s filming infrastructure and have thrown support behind FilmLEX in the past. These efforts at the local level are in addition to the state’s own initiatives to encourage production to relocate to Kentucky. Via the Kentucky Entertainment Initiative Program, the state offers a fully refundable, non-transferable tax credit ranging from 30% to 35%. The program has an annual funding cap of $75 million and per project cap of $10 million.
